relations.note: Homer calls Ate Zeus’s powerful daughter, perhaps his eldest or most venerable.

relations.myth: Ate blinds Zeus during Hera’s birth scheme
relations.note: Ate’s delusion prevents Zeus from detecting Hera’s manipulation of the royal birth.
Zeus seizes Ate by her hair and permanently hurls her into the mortal world.
Hesiod makes Ate a fatherless daughter of Eris among destructive personifications.
Aeschylus metaphorically calls ruinous Peitho the child of designing Ate.

relations.myth: The Litai follow and remedy Ate
relations.note: The slow Litai pursue swift Ate, healing her damage or requesting her punishment of the unreceptive.

relations.myth: Hera manipulates births while Ate blinds Zeus
relations.note: Hera benefits from Zeus’s delusion, although Homer records no command, meeting, or conspiracy with Ate.

relations.myth: Ate deceives Ampelus to gratify Hera
relations.note: Ate executes a fatal deception to please Hera, Dionysus’s hostile stepmother.

relations.myth: Manipulation of Heracles’ and Eurystheus’s births
relations.note: The birth deity advances Hera’s scheme while Ate accounts for Zeus’s blindness; no direct interaction occurs.
By deluding Zeus, Ate enables Hera’s scheme transferring the promised kingship from Heracles to Eurystheus.

relations.myth: Ate causes the death of Dionysus’s beloved
relations.note: Ate indirectly harms Dionysus by deceiving his beloved Ampelus into a fatal bull ride.

relations.myth: Ate tricks Ampelus into riding a bull
relations.note: Disguised as his companion, Ate exploits Ampelus’s insecurity and persuades him to ride a bull.
Ate’s deception causes Ampelus to mount a bull, fall, and die.

relations.myth: Dike observes while Ate punishes insolence
relations.note: Dike sits above while Ate punishes shameless speech, without a narrated meeting.

relations.myth: Hybris and Ate attend the third wine-bowl
relations.note: The third wine-bowl jointly brings Hybris and Ate, marking excessive drinking’s ruinous consequences.
